concept.name: Bear flattener
concept.definition: A flattening of the yield curve driven by short-term interest rates rising faster than long-term rates. It is called 'bear' because rising yields mean falling bond prices, and the pattern typically appears when the central bank is raising short-term policy rates.
concept.intuition: The curve flattens from the front end selling off: short rates rise faster than long rates, usually as the central bank hikes.
concept.mechanics: Classified by decomposing the spread change: the front-end yield rises faster than the back-end yield, narrowing or inverting the spread. A flattener position (short front leg, long back leg) gains, with the short front leg capturing most of the move as policy-rate expectations re-price.
concept.formula: Condition: Δy_short > 0 and Δ(y_long - y_short) < 0, i.e. the front-end yield rises faster than the back-end yield.
concept.failure_modes: Descriptive, not predictive: bear flattening late in a hiking cycle often precedes a sharp bull flattener or bull steepener, so extrapolating the pattern is hazardous. Persistent inversion can also create carry drag on flattener positions held through long plateaus.
concept.misconceptions: A bear flattener does not require long rates to fall — they usually rise too, just less than short rates. Curve inversion produced by bear flattening is a descriptive state, not a mechanical guarantee of recession.
concept.example: During an aggressive hiking cycle the 2-year yield climbs from 3.0% to 5.0% while the 10-year rises only from 3.2% to 4.2%; the 2s10s spread narrows from +20 bp to -80 bp — a bear flattener.

citations.source: LearnBonds: Bull Flattener, Bear Flattener, Bull Steepener and Bear Steepener Explained
